_comment: Hand-written narrative entries. This is the one part of the site that is not
derived from the change log, because it is the part that requires judgement:
the data can show that 13,600 work orders stopped being published, but only a
person can say what that probably means and what it does not prove.
Add an entry when something happens that would otherwise leave a reader
puzzled by a number, or when a claim on the site needs its reasoning shown.
Every figure quoted here must be reproducible from data/deltas/.
Inline markup in any text: **bold**, *italic*, `code`, [label](url). Nothing
else — entries are trusted repo content, but a small vocabulary keeps them plain.

entries.title: “Repair Complete” does not mean the repair is complete
entries.summary: A third closed-feed status that reads like an outcome and is not one. Four in five records carrying it still show outstanding work on Thames Water's own count — and that count usually goes up, not down, at the moment it is applied.

body.p: If you look up your street on Thames Water's map and see **Repair Complete**, the natural reading is that the job is done. On the evidence in their own feed, it usually is not.

Every work order carries a count of *line items* — the individual tasks making up the job — split into open and closed. Comparing that count against the status is revealing, because two of Thames Water's statuses are clean and one is not:

**A twenty-eight-fold difference between two statuses that sound like the same thing.** The same split shows among faults still on the map: of 447 currently marked *Repair Complete*, 378 have outstanding line items, which puts them alongside *Repair Underway* (91.6%) rather than *Completed* (0%).

The timing is harder to explain away than the totals. We have watched work orders move into *Repair Complete* 947 times. In **688** of them, the number of open line items **went up** in the same moment — the record gained outstanding work at the instant it was declared finished. It fell in only 203.
One example from the change log, with times as collected:

list: `13:45` — open line items go **1 → 4**, and status moves *Repair Underway* → *Repair Complete*
`15:31` — a further line item closes; the completion timestamp is revised two hours later than first published

body.p: Planning to complete in seventy-six minutes, with the job's total line items going from four to eight. That work order's type is *Visible Leak **Investigation***, which points at the likeliest explanation: the **investigation** finished and the **repair** was raised at the same instant, and the single work-order status reports the first of those. A resident of that street separately reported an open excavation, barriers and Thames Water signage on site, and had that same day received notice from Thames Water that the repair was still to be done.

*Repair Complete* also behaves like a waiting room rather than an ending — and how long a wait depends on which clock you read. Thames Water's own completion stamp on these records is never more than about three days old. The records themselves have been showing *Repair Complete* for considerably longer:

head: Time at “Repair Complete”, measured from
Median
Longest
Over a week
rows: When we watched the status actually change

body.p: **63 faults have been publicly showing a finished status for over a week**, the longest for ten and a half days, while the timestamp beside them never reads older than three. The reason is that the timestamp is not a completion time at all: **it is continually pushed forward.** Of 1,093 records that have had one set, 751 — 68.7% — were later revised, across 2,001 separate revisions. **Every single one moved the time later. Not one moved it earlier.** The typical jump is fifteen hours; some records have been revised eight times or more.

And it moves in step with the line items above. 94.1% of those revisions land in the same update as a change to the count of *closed* line items, and **every one of those is an increase**. In 1,469 of them, open line items remained above zero afterwards. So the stamp appears to track the most recently finished task on the job, not the finishing of the job — each task that completes pushes it forward, which restarts the 72-hour countdown that removes the pin from the map. That is why 434 of the 447 records currently at *Repair Complete* carry a stamp less than 72 hours old while some have been sitting there for a week and a half.

**What has changed here.** This site no longer counts *Repair Complete* as an outcome. It moves from “faults we can account for” to “no outcome published”, which moves 382 records and changes the cancelled share of explained departures from 12.7% to 13.8%. On the Faults tab, any fault whose status sounds finished while its own line-item count says otherwise is now marked.

**What this does not prove.** Thames Water does not document what a line item is, so an open one is not direct evidence that a hole is unfilled. The claim rests on the contrast — 79.8% against 2.8% — and on the direction the counter moves, both of which anyone can reproduce from the change log. The eyewitness account is what prompted the check; it is not what the finding stands on. Nor does any of this show that a *repair* took ten days: what was observed is that the record showed a finished status for ten days, which is a claim about what the public was told, not about what is in the ground. It is also possible this is an artefact of how a repair job is split from an investigation job internally, in which case the status is not dishonest so much as useless to a member of the public reading it.

refs.label: Issue #32 — the working, the queries, and the caveats

entries.title: Thames Water mostly meets the deadlines it sets itself — on the small jobs
entries.summary: Their own road-opening permits are now published here. Four out of five completed works finished by the date they applied for; the exceptions are concentrated in the big schemes.

body.p: Before Thames Water can dig up a road, it has to apply to the highway authority for a permit saying when the work will start and finish. The Department for Transport publishes those applications, and the dates the work actually started and stopped. That makes a question askable that the fault map alone cannot answer: **when they finally did the work, did it finish when they said it would?**
This is a deadline Thames Water set for itself, in an application it wrote, to a regulator that can issue fixed penalty notices. It is a fairer test than most — and on the whole they pass it.

head: Against the end date they applied for
Works
Share
rows: Finished on the last permitted day

body.p: From 16,653 permits published for July 2026, of which 7,796 record both a proposed and an actual end. **Roughly one in five completed works finished late, but almost all of those by a single day.** Only 83 ran more than a day over. The worst was 43 days.

That single-day figure deserves a caveat rather than a headline. A job finishing at nine the morning after its permit expired is counted late here, and in a working sense it very nearly was not. What the number does rule out is a picture of routine, sustained overrunning on ordinary repairs.
The pattern underneath is more interesting than the total, because the late rate is not spread evenly:

Urgent and emergency work — the burst main, the flooded street — is the most likely to finish on time. Major planned schemes are three and a half times more likely to run over. The same gradient shows against how long the work actually took: 17% of jobs under a day ran late, against 43% of jobs lasting more than a month.

**That gradient is why the 21% should be read as a floor.** Only works that finished inside a published month can be measured at all, so long jobs are under-counted — and long jobs are exactly the ones that overrun. The true rate across all work is higher than this, by an amount we cannot measure from one month.
Two things this does *not* show, stated plainly because both are easy to assume:

list: **It says nothing about any particular fault on the map.** We built the obvious join — permit within so many metres of a fault, within so many days — and tested it by shuffling which fault sits at which location. At its best it fired about five times more often than chance while reaching only 1% of faults, so about one in five surviving matches was still coincidence. Thames Water digs where its pipes are and its faults are where its pipes are, so being near a permit means much less than it looks. The join is built and is not published.

**It says nothing about the wait before the work.** A permit records what happened once the digging was scheduled. A fault sitting at *Repair Planning* for eight months and then repaired in the two days its permit allowed counts here as on time, because it was. The delay this site mostly documents happens before a permit is ever applied for.

body.p: One aside worth recording: 2,959 of Thames Water's 16,653 permits — about 18% — carry no map coordinates at all, and those are disproportionately the Major and Standard schemes — the ones that overrun most. Any analysis that starts by requiring a location is therefore blind to the worst-behaved works. That is a trap rather than a conspiracy, but it is worth knowing about.
The June 2026 archive is excluded: the file on DfT's server is truncated where it was uploaded, ending part-way through a filename, and a partial month would carry a hole of unknown size.

refs.label: Issue #6 — the permit join, the null model, and why it is not published

entries.title: A third of the links between reports and repairs are coincidence
entries.summary: We tested the site's own matching by shuffling the addresses. It fires far more often on chance than we had claimed.

body.p: When you look up a problem someone reported, this site tries to show you the work order that followed it. Neither feed carries a reference number the other shares, so the link is inferred: a report and a work order on the same street, within a few days of each other.
We previously said 99–100% of those links were genuine. **That was wrong**, and it was wrong because of how we tested it.

The old test kept each report's address and moved its date by a month or more. Anything still matching had to be coincidence. It looked reassuring — almost nothing matched. But Thames Water raises far more work in August than in May, roughly 218 jobs a day against 112, so moving a report backwards in time put it against a thinner field and made chance look rarer than it is. Moving reports *forward* was worse still: it pushed them past the end of our data, where nothing could match at all.

The better test keeps every date exactly where it is and **shuffles which address belongs to which report**. Every report then faces precisely the same amount of work being raised as it really did. The only thing broken is the pairing of place and time — which is the entire thing the matching claims to detect.

So on the week-long window the site was using, **about half the links would have appeared anyway**. Not because the matching is broken, but because a busy street gets work regardless of who reported what. Take a street with a leak reported on Tuesday and unrelated sewer work booked for Thursday, and this site would have drawn a line between them.

The window is now **three days**, which is where the number of links actually caused by a report is highest. Going out to a week added 114 real links and 394 coincidental ones — it was making the picture worse, not fuller. About a third of what remains is still chance, and the site now says so next to every link rather than describing it vaguely as an association.

**What this means if you are looking up your own report.** A link shown here is a reason to ask Thames Water a question, not an answer. If the work order is at your address and appeared the day after you reported, that is fairly strong. If it is further down the street and three days later, it may have nothing to do with you.

Two smaller faults turned up while checking this. Work orders that had been completed were being listed twice, so **787 reports were told their match was ambiguous when only one work order was involved** — the site was inventing doubt in the one place it tries hardest not to guess. And links to work orders that had already left the map were rendered as though you could click through to them, which did nothing. Both fixed.

None of this changes how many reports become work orders, which is still the thing we cannot honestly tell you. Reports with no address cannot be matched at all, a job may be recorded at a neighbour's address, and a report about a problem already logged may never generate a work order of its own while still being acted on.

refs.label: Issue #1 — the working, and what a conversion rate still needs

entries.title: A job can be finished a day before their map admits it
entries.summary: A work order stays on Thames Water's map for exactly 24 or 72 hours after they close it. And departures are now almost always confirmed — up from about 70% before.

body.p: Two things have changed in how much this site can tell you, and both are worth knowing if you are watching a problem of your own.

**A closed job lingers on the map.** Every work order carries a field saying how many hours it should remain on the map. It turns out to mean exactly that, and it is now measurable: comparing Thames Water's own closure timestamp against the moment a record actually stopped being published gives an extremely tight answer.

So a fault still shown as open on their map may have been closed up to a day ago — three days for the minority set to 72 hours. The extra two hours are our own hourly checking, not theirs. If you are watching a job, the disappearance is the *last* signal you get, not the first.

It also means this site has been overstating how long repairs take, because it measured to the day a record vanished rather than the day it was closed. The gap is about **1.1 days** on a typical case. That is small against a median measured in weeks, but it is a bias in one direction and it is now known.

**Departures are now nearly always confirmed.** When a work order leaves the map, Thames Water's separate closed feed may or may not confirm what happened to it. That confirmation has improved sharply over the past week:

head: Work orders leaving the map on
Number
Confirmed by the closed feed

body.p: Over the same week the closed feed roughly tripled — waste water from about 1,500 records to 4,644, clean water from about 500 to 2,171. Whether Thames Water started publishing more of it or simply kept it for longer, we cannot tell from outside. The effect either way is that **"cleared" on this site now usually means something**: for most departures there is now a *Completed* or *Canceled* verdict behind it rather than a record that merely stopped appearing.
That is a real improvement in what can honestly be said here, and it is Thames Water's doing, not ours.

**The 5 August losses have still not returned.** The map has carried between roughly 7,000 and 7,350 open work orders every day since, standing at 7,346 today. No further collection has been flagged: whatever happened that evening happened once.

**A correction, while fixing the charts.** The headline "typical time to clear" on this site has been badly wrong, and it has now moved from 22 days to **3 days**. The 5 August losses were mostly work that had been open for months, and counting the moment they stopped being published as the moment they were fixed put a 72-day median into the figure. It was measuring a data loss as though it were repairs.

3 days is the honest number: departures before the event ran to a median of 1.5 days and those after it to 3.0 days, so the corrected figure sits where both cohorts already were. The 22 days was an artefact throughout. Those 13,446 uncorroborated departures are still recorded and still browsable — they are simply no longer counted as evidence of anything being fixed, and the figure now says how many it leaves out.

refs.label: Issue #29 — the working behind these figures

entries.title: Leaks sit for years. Sewage problems do not.
entries.summary: 800 clean water work orders have been open for more than a year. The waste water figure is 21.

body.p: Thames Water's map covers two networks: clean water — the pipes bringing water to you — and waste water, the sewers taking it away. Set side by side, the work outstanding on each looks nothing alike.
These are counts of work Thames Water is publishing as open right now, measured from its own raised date:

**510 of the year-old clean water cases are visible leak investigations** — water coming out of the ground somewhere, reported, logged, and still logged a year later. The oldest open clean water work order was raised in March 2024.
The obvious objection is that this is an artefact of how the map works rather than a fact about the work, so we checked three ways before publishing it.

list: **It is not the 5 August data loss.** Before that event clean water had 977 work orders over a year old and waste water had 21. Waste water still has exactly 21. The gap predates it entirely.

**There is no cutoff removing old sewer work.** If the map dropped waste water records past a certain age, none would survive to be old — but 8 waste water work orders have been open over two years, and the oldest dates from August 2023. Old sewer work can stay on the map. There is just very little of it.
**These are not estimates.** They are counts of the records on the map today, not a sample or a projection.

body.p: What it most likely reflects is triage, and there is a reasonable version of that: a blocked sewer or sewage flooding a garden forces action within days, while a leak that is merely wasting water can be left on a list. Both readings — that sewage work is genuinely dealt with quickly, and that leaks are genuinely tolerated for years — are consistent with the same numbers.

What the figures do *not* show is whether the leak is still leaking. A work order staying open means Thames Water has not closed it, not that water is still running today. Nor can we say how much water is involved: the feed carries no volume, and a year-old *investigation* is not the same as a year-old known leak.
If you reported a leak and it is still on their map months later, that is not unusual. It is the normal condition of several hundred cases.

refs.label: Issue #27 — the check-in, and what was deliberately not published

entries.title: Three days on, the missing work orders have not come back
entries.summary: The map has settled at about 7,200 open work orders and stayed there. Ordinary service resumed — over a much smaller published set.

body.p: Following the collapse of 5 August, described in the entry below, the map has now been read 44 more times. Open work orders have stayed between 7,197 and 7,661 throughout, and stood at **7,222** at the most recent collection. Waste water is still at 13.7% of the size it was that morning. Nothing has been restored.

The useful new evidence is that everything *else* went back to normal. When a work order leaves the map, Thames Water's separate closed feed usually confirms within a day that it was completed or cancelled. That confirmation rate collapsed during the event and has since recovered:

That tells us something worth knowing: this was **a single episode of loss, not a system that is still broken**. Records are being created, updated and closed normally again. They are simply doing it over a set of published work orders about a third the previous size.

**The practical point for anyone using their map.** A fault disappearing from it is not evidence that anyone fixed it. That is always somewhat true — this site exists partly to say so — but on the evening of 5 August it was true roughly 13,600 times at once. If a problem you reported stopped appearing that evening, the disappearance carries no information about the work.
Your reference number is unaffected. It is Thames Water's record, not the map's, and remains the thing to quote when asking them directly.

We still cannot say what caused it, and expect not to be able to. From outside, a service reporting 1,386 rows because the system feeding it failed looks exactly like one reporting 1,386 rows because that is genuinely all there is.

entries.title: Two thirds of the backlog stopped being published
entries.summary: Thames Water's map lost 13,600 open work orders in a single evening. Almost none of it is corroborated as work done.

body.p: On the morning of 5 August, Thames Water's public map carried **20,477** open work orders. By that evening it carried **7,350**. Clean water went first — the 18:47 collection found it down from 9,680 to 5,615. Waste water followed two hours later, collapsing from 10,855 to **1,386**, 13% of what it had held that morning. It settled at about 7,600 over the following hours and did not recover; see the later entries for where it stands now.
This site records what their feed publishes, so the drop is shown as it happened. What follows is why we do not think it means the work was done.

**Their own closed feed does not corroborate it.** Thames Water separately publishes work orders it has finished with, marked *Completed* or *Canceled*. Before this event, 66.9% of faults that left the map turned up there within a day. For these departures:
The closed feed did grow — it gained 1,600 records at 00:46 — but only 367 of those are work orders that departed in this event. It is a different set of records, not the missing ones arriving.

**The wrong records went.** If thousands of jobs had been completed, they would have moved into the finished states. Instead the finished states are almost the only thing that survived, while work still in progress was wiped:

**They were not renumbered either.** A system migration could give the same faults new reference numbers, which would look like mass departure followed by mass arrival. Matching departures against later arrivals on street, postcode and Thames Water's own raised time finds only 28 matches out of 1,202 — and every one is the same record returning under an identical `WorkOrderID`. These are reappearances, not renamed faults.

**Nor is it a cutoff by age.** The oldest surviving open faults still date from August 2023 and March 2024. Of roughly 13,600 departures, 190 have ever come back. The loss was close to indiscriminate: 70–90% gone across every problem type, every priority flag and both networks.
What it did change is the shape of what remains. The middle of the distribution was hollowed out, and the proportion of very old work actually doubled:

**What we think happened.** Most likely a publication or data pipeline failure at Thames Water's end that has persisted rather than healed. We can rule out a fault on our side: each layer is checked against the row count Thames Water's own service advertises, and every retrieval through this period was complete. Their service really is serving these numbers.

What we cannot do is prove it. A layer that reports 1,386 rows because the system feeding it broke looks identical, from outside, to one that reports 1,386 rows because that is the truth. That distinction needs someone inside Thames Water, or an answer to a formal information request.

**What this site does about it.** All 13,600 departures are recorded and browsable under Faults → Cleared, where they show as *Not confirmed*. They are held out of the time-to-fix figures unless the closed feed corroborates them, so that a single event at the source cannot quietly rewrite every average here. The number excluded is published alongside.
